source.title: The Bābur-nāma in English (Memoirs of Bābur)
source.attribution: Babur, The Bābur-nāma in English (Memoirs of Bābur) (trans. Annette Susannah Beveridge), Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: Babur became a king at eleven when his father fell from a ravine
cards.body:
In June 1494, in the fort of Akhsi in the Ferghana Valley (in today's Uzbekistan), Babur's father Umar Shaikh Mirza was at his pigeon-house on the edge of a deep ravine when the building gave way and he fell to his death. Babur, aged eleven, was in a garden in the town of Andijan. Within days he was ruler of a small, fertile kingdom, with two uncles already marching against it.

Babur records the moment with a poet's phrase: his father 'became a falcon'. Life sometimes hands people responsibility long before they feel ready. Babur's story begins there, not with a plan but with a sudden loss he had to grow into.
cards.quote: Umar Shaikh Mīrzā flew, with his pigeons and their house, and became a falcon.
cards.apply_it: Think of a responsibility that arrived before you felt ready. Name one person who helped you carry it, and thank them this week.

quiz.question: How did Babur become ruler of Ferghana in 1494?
options: He defeated his father in battle
His father died when the pigeon-house above a ravine collapsed
He was elected by the people of Samarkand
His uncle handed him the throne
quiz.explanation: His father fell to his death at Akhsi, and eleven-year-old Babur inherited the kingdom.

cards.title: A child king survived because his father's men held together
cards.body:
When eleven-year-old Babur took the throne, one noble grabbed his bridle to lead him out of Andijan, fearing the town would hand him over to an invading uncle. Others called him back into the citadel and set about strengthening the walls. His uncle Sultan Ahmad Mirza of Samarkand came within a few miles, then turned back: horses and camels had drowned at a crowded bridge, disease struck his horses, and he found the defenders united and ready to give their lives.

Babur credits his father's old officers, who held resolutely together. A group under pressure is strongest when people stop looking after only themselves. In a crisis, holding together often matters more than having a perfect plan.
cards.quote: Umar Shaikh Mīrzā's former begs and braves had held resolutely together and made daring offer of their lives.
cards.apply_it: Next time your team or family is under pressure, ask out loud: what must we hold together on, whatever else changes?

quiz.question: Which of these helped turn back the uncle's army from Andijan, according to Babur?
options: The defenders' unity, plus losses on the march
quiz.explanation: Babur lists drowned animals, sick horses and the single-minded resolve of his soldiers and peasants.

cards.title: His father returned a lost caravan's goods though he badly needed money
cards.body:
Babur describes his father as short, stout and fond of tunics so tight the strings tore, but he also tells a story of quiet honesty. A caravan from China was buried by snow in the mountains east of Andijan, and of a thousand households only two people survived. Umar Shaikh Mirza had the goods collected and kept safe. Though no heirs were near and he was short of money himself, he sent for the families in Khurasan and Samarkand and within a year or two handed everything back.

No one would have known if he had kept it. Integrity is mostly tested in moments like that, when the gain is real and nobody is watching.
cards.quote: summoned the heirs from Khurāsān and Samarkand, and in the course of a year or two had made over to them all their property safe and sound.
cards.apply_it: Is there something you hold that isn't really yours, like a borrowed item, an unearned credit or a small debt? Return or settle it this week.

quiz.question: What did Babur's father do with the goods of the snowbound caravan?
options: Kept them safe and returned them to the owners' heirs
Used them to pay his army
quiz.explanation: Even though he was in want himself, he summoned the heirs and returned all their property.

cards.title: Babur described his own father's faults as plainly as his virtues
cards.body:
Most royal memoirs flatter the family. Babur's does not. He calls his father generous, eloquent, brave, devout and good company, then adds that he drank heavily in his youth, lost his head under intoxicating sweets later on, and played dice. Above all, he says his father's appetite for conquest kept dragging the little kingdom into war: he marched on Samarkand again and again and was often beaten.

Seeing a parent whole, gifts and flaws together, is a mark of maturity. It lets you keep the good you inherited and choose consciously what you will do differently.
cards.quote: Through his ambition, peace was exchanged often for war, friendliness for hostility.
cards.apply_it: Write two lines about a parent or mentor: one quality you want to carry on, and one pattern you choose to leave behind.

quiz.question: What did Babur say his father's ambition often cost?
options: His friendship with his own father
quiz.explanation: Babur wrote that through his father's ambition, peace was often exchanged for war and friendliness for hostility.

cards.title: The teenage king leaned openly on his grandmother's judgment
cards.body:
In Babur's first year as ruler, an officer named Hasan-i-Yaqub began behaving as if he would depose Babur and put his younger half-brother Jahangir in his place. Babur's loyal supporters met in the presence of his grandmother, Aisan-daulat Begim, widow of the Mongol Khan Yunus, and decided to remove the plotter before he could act.

In chronicles full of men and battles, Babur goes out of his way to praise her as very wise and far-sighted, and says most of his affairs were carried through under her advice. Good leaders know whose judgment they trust, and they are not too proud to say so.
cards.quote: Few amongst women will have been my grandmother's equals for judgment and counsel; she was very wise and far-sighted and most affairs of mine were carried through under her advice.
cards.apply_it: Name the person whose judgment you trust most. Before your next big decision, ask them what they would do and why.

quiz.question: Whose advice did young Babur say guided most of his affairs?
quiz.explanation: Babur praised his grandmother's judgment and counsel above almost anyone's.

cards.title: Winning Samarkand at fourteen brought hunger, not riches
cards.body:
In late 1497, after a seven-month siege, the fourteen-year-old Babur took Samarkand, the great city of his ancestor Timur in today's Uzbekistan. It should have been a triumph. But the countryside had already been raided bare, and the city itself was so distressed that it needed seed-corn and loans rather than taxes. Babur had nothing to give his soldiers. Homesick and unpaid, they began slipping away in ones and twos, the Mongol troops first of all.

Getting the prize is not the same as being able to keep it. Before chasing a big goal, ask how you will sustain it, and what the people who helped you will need once you arrive.
cards.quote: When we entered the town, it was in such distress that it needed seed-corn and money-advances; what place was this to take anything from?
cards.apply_it: Pick a goal you are working towards. Write down what it will take to keep it going for a year after you reach it.

quiz.question: Why did Babur's soldiers start leaving him after he took Samarkand in 1497?
options: The city was too poor to reward them and they missed home
They were defeated by the Uzbeks
quiz.explanation: The city needed seed-corn and loans, so there was nothing to give the men, and they drifted home.

cards.title: Rushing to save one city, Babur lost both
cards.body:
While holding Samarkand in early 1498, Babur fell so ill that for four days he could not speak and water was dripped into his mouth with cotton. His officers, by what he calls an error of judgment, let an enemy messenger see him like this. The man carried the story to Andijan, where the commander Ali-dost, told the king was dying, surrendered the city. Begged by his mother and grandmother to come home, Babur left Samarkand after a hundred days of rule, only to learn on the road that Andijan had fallen the very day he set out.

A careless moment and a rumour did the damage. Guard what others see in a weak moment, and check bad news before acting on it.
cards.quote: In anxiety for Andijān, we had given Samarkand out of our hands; then heard we had lost Andijān.
cards.apply_it: The next time alarming news reaches you second-hand, confirm it with one direct source before you react.

quiz.question: What triggered the surrender of Andijan in 1498?
options: A report that Babur was dying, spread after an enemy messenger saw him ill
quiz.explanation: The messenger reported Babur speechless and near death, and the commander Ali-dost used this as his excuse to surrender.

cards.title: A young king admitted he cried, then kept going
cards.body:
By the spring of 1498 Babur had lost both Samarkand and his home kingdom. Most of his officers' families were in Andijan, so seven or eight hundred men left him to go home, leaving two or three hundred companions in exile. Babur, about fifteen, does not dress this up. He writes that it came very hard on him and that he could not help crying a good deal. Then he went back to the poor town of Khujand and began planning again.

Tears are not the opposite of strength. Babur's honesty shows that grief and determination can sit side by side: you can feel a loss fully and still take the next step.
cards.quote: It came very hard on me; I could not help crying a good deal.
cards.apply_it: If something is weighing on you, give yourself ten minutes to feel it fully, then write down one small next step.

quiz.question: How did Babur react when most of his men left him in 1498?
options: He gave up his claim to rule
He admitted he cried a good deal, then regrouped in Khujand
quiz.explanation: He openly recorded his tears, and then returned to Khujand to plan his next move.

cards.title: Babur refused to sit still after one or two failures
cards.body:
From his base in Khujand in 1498, Babur tried again and again. An allied army set out with him for Samarkand and turned back. He borrowed troops from his uncle, the Mongol Khan of Tashkent, stormed a small fort, and was then told, rightly, that holding one fort led nowhere. Chapter after chapter ends the same way: back to Khujand. Yet within a year he had won back Marghinan and then Andijan.

Babur names his own driving force honestly: ambition. Whatever moves you, the lesson holds. Early attempts that go nowhere are part of the road, not proof that the road is closed.
cards.quote: As there was in me ambition for rule and desire of conquest, I did not sit at gaze when once or twice an affair had made no progress.
cards.apply_it: Think of a goal you dropped after one or two failed tries. What is one fresh attempt you could make this month?

quiz.question: What did Babur say kept him trying after repeated failures in 1498?
quiz.explanation: He wrote that ambition for rule kept him from sitting idle when an attempt made no progress.

cards.title: Do your worrying before you set out, not halfway there
cards.body:
In 1499, wandering and nearly hopeless, Babur received a message from Ali-dost, the very commander who had surrendered Andijan, offering to hand over the fort of Marghinan. Babur rode at once, three nights and two days without rest. Just short of the fort his officers raised a fair point: Ali-dost had betrayed them before, and nothing had been agreed. Babur judged that the worry was reasonable but had come too late; the horses were spent and there was nowhere to turn back to. They went on, and Marghinan was theirs.

Do your doubting at the decision point. Once committed, second thoughts mostly drain the strength you need to finish.
cards.quote: reasonable as anxiety was, it ought to have been earlier
cards.apply_it: Before your next commitment, spend 15 minutes listing every doubt. Then decide, and park new doubts until a set review date.

quiz.question: What did Babur conclude about his officers' doubts near Marghinan?
options: They should turn back at once
The doubts were reasonable but should have been raised earlier
The doubts proved Ali-dost was loyal
quiz.explanation: Having ridden so far, turning back made no sense; worry was useful only before setting out.

cards.title: A fair-looking order can still spark a rebellion
cards.body:
After recovering Andijan in 1499, Babur let the rebel commander leave unharmed but allowed his own loyal men to take back goods that the rebels' followers had looted from them. It seemed just. But the order frightened the Mongol troops in his service, who feared they would be stripped next. They went over to his rival Tambal, and Babur later traced his second loss of Andijan to that one hasty order.

His lesson is worth keeping: something can look reasonable and fair on the surface and still need many careful thoughts about its knock-on effects. Before acting, ask not only 'is this right?' but 'how will each group hear it?'
cards.quote: In conquest and government, though many things may have an outside appearance of reason and justice, yet 100,000 reflections are right and necessary as to the bearings of each one of them.
cards.apply_it: Before announcing your next decision, list everyone it touches and write one line on how each might read it.

quiz.question: Why did Babur regret his order to let his men reclaim looted goods?
options: It frightened the Mongol troops, who rebelled
His men refused to obey it
quiz.explanation: Though just on its face, it alarmed the Mongols, and Babur blamed it for his second exile from Andijan.

cards.title: With 240 men and some ladders, Babur retook Samarkand by night
cards.body:
In 1500 the Uzbek leader Shaibani Khan seized Samarkand. Babur, by his own count nineteen and holding almost nothing, judged that the city had not yet accepted its new master. After one failed approach he tried again. At midnight seventy or eighty of his men climbed the walls by ladders, killed the guards at the Turquoise Gate and opened it. By dawn townspeople were bringing food and prayers, while in the lanes several hundred Uzbek soldiers were beaten to death by the crowd.

A small, determined group acting at the right moment can do what a large, hesitant one cannot. It can also set loose violence no one fully controls.
cards.quote: With 240 proved men I had taken Samarkand
cards.apply_it: Is there a goal you are waiting to have more resources for? Ask what a small, well-timed first move would look like.

quiz.question: How did Babur's men get into Samarkand in 1500?
options: By climbing the walls with ladders at night and opening a gate
quiz.explanation: About seventy or eighty men climbed by ladder, took the Turquoise Gate and let Babur in.

cards.title: Babur lost a battle by rushing to fight on a 'lucky' day
cards.body:
In spring 1501 Babur marched out of Samarkand to face Shaibani Khan at Sar-i-pul. Reinforcements were close: one or two thousand men from Kesh within a couple of days, more from his uncle by the next dawn. He fought anyway, because a star sign was said to favour him that day. The Uzbeks wheeled round behind his lines, his allied Mongol troops plundered his own men, and Babur escaped only by swimming his horse, both in armour, across a flooded river.

Later he wrote that such considerations were worth nothing. Signs and self-imposed deadlines can push us to act before we are ready. Waiting two days for help rarely costs as much as losing everything in a hurry.
cards.quote: I now understand that these considerations are worth nothing and that our haste was without reason.
cards.apply_it: Is a deadline you have set yourself real, or arbitrary? If waiting a few days would make you much stronger, consider waiting.

quiz.question: Why did Babur hurry into battle at Sar-i-pul?
options: A star sign was said to favour him that day
quiz.explanation: He fought early for astrological reasons, and later called that haste groundless.

cards.title: No one helped him in defeat, because no one helped him in strength
cards.body:
After Sar-i-pul, Shaibani Khan besieged Babur inside Samarkand through the summer of 1501. The poorest people ate dogs and donkeys; horses were fed on mulberry leaves and wood shavings. Babur sent envoys in every direction, including to the powerful Sultan Husain Mirza of Herat, but no help came. His own reflection is clear-eyed: no one had come when he was strong and unbeaten, so why would they come now? At last he accepted terms and slipped out at midnight.

Support networks are built in good times. The friendships and goodwill you invest in while things go well are the ones that answer when they do not.
cards.quote: No-one had helped or reinforced me when I was in strength and power and had suffered no sort of defeat or loss; on what score would any-one help me now?
cards.apply_it: This week, reach out to one person in your network just to help or catch up, with nothing to ask of them.

quiz.question: What did Babur conclude when no allies came to relieve Samarkand?
options: His allies were secretly on their way
No one had helped him when he was strong, so none would help him weak
quiz.explanation: He reasoned that those who gave nothing in his strength had even less reason to help in his weakness.

cards.title: Leaving Samarkand cost Babur his sister for ten years
cards.body:
When Babur left besieged Samarkand in 1501, his elder sister Khanzada Begim fell into the hands of the victor, Shaibani Khan, and became his wife. Babur mentions it in a line, but the loss stayed with him. After Shah Ismail of Persia defeated the Uzbeks near Merv in 1510, the Shah sent Khanzada back to Babur with an escort. When Babur went to see her, after some ten years apart, neither she nor her household recognised him, even when he spoke.

Wars are told as maps and battles, but their costs fall on families. Time also changes people more than we expect, which is a reason not to put off the visits that matter.
cards.quote: We had been apart for some ten years; when Muḥammadī kūkūldāsh and I went to see her, neither she nor those about her knew us, although I spoke.
cards.apply_it: Is there a relative or old friend you have not seen for years? Arrange a call or visit this month.

quiz.question: What happened when Babur was reunited with his sister Khanzada?
options: Neither she nor her household recognised him at first
She had become queen of Persia
She asked him to retake Samarkand
quiz.explanation: After about ten years apart, they did not know him even when he spoke; they recognised him after a while.

cards.title: Ordinary comfort tastes best right after hardship
cards.body:
Escaping Samarkand by night in 1501, Babur's small party got lost among irrigation channels. Racing with friends, his saddle slipped and he was thrown on his head; until evening the world felt like a dream. They killed and roasted a horse to eat. Then they reached the town of Dizak, where there was fat meat, fine bread, sweet melons and grapes. Babur says that never in his life had he appreciated safety and plenty so much.

He noticed something true about the mind: contrast sharpens joy. We cannot always choose our hardships, but afterwards we can pause to notice the simple comforts that return, a hot meal, a safe bed, a quiet morning.
cards.quote: Joy is best and more delightful when it follows sorrow, ease after toil.
cards.apply_it: After your next hard day, take two minutes to name three ordinary comforts you have tonight.

quiz.question: What did Babur learn from reaching Dizak after fleeing Samarkand?
options: That cities are safer than villages
That joy is sweetest after sorrow
quiz.explanation: He wrote that joy is best when it follows sorrow, and ease after toil.

cards.title: A 111-year-old village woman linked Babur to Timur's age
cards.body:
In the winter of 1501 to 1502, the exiled Babur stayed in Dikh-kat, a village of shepherds in the hills near Ura-tube in today's Tajikistan. He lodged with the headman, a man of seventy or eighty whose mother was still alive at 111. She remembered, and liked to tell, how a relative of hers had gone with Timur's army to India more than a century before. Ninety-six of her descendants lived in that village alone.

Babur, Timur's own descendant, was hearing his family's history from a peasant woman's memory. The oldest people around us are living archives, and their stories vanish unless someone sits down and listens.
cards.quote: She was a woman on whom much life had been bestowed for she was 111 years old.
cards.apply_it: Ask the oldest person you know to tell you one story from their childhood, and write it down afterwards.

quiz.question: What story did the 111-year-old woman of Dikh-kat like to tell?
options: How a relative went to India with Timur's army
How she once ruled the village
quiz.explanation: She kept in mind and retold the tale of a relative who went with Timur's army to India.

cards.title: Walking barefoot through exile hardened Babur's feet and spirit
cards.body:
In the same village, with no kingdom and few men, Babur spent his days roaming the mountains. He usually went barefoot, and did it so often that rock and stone stopped hurting. Once, unsure of a path at dusk, he told his companions to keep their eyes on a cow going down a narrow track and follow it to see where the road came out. One of them joked: and if the cow loses her way, what becomes of us?

Hardship toughens us in small, literal ways, and humour keeps a group human while it happens. You do not have to wait for good times to build strength, or to laugh.
cards.quote: Generally I went bare-foot and, from doing this so much, my feet became so that rock and stone made no difference to them.
cards.apply_it: Choose one small, safe discomfort to practise this week, such as walking instead of driving, and notice how quickly you adapt.

quiz.question: What did Babur notice after months of going barefoot in the hills?
options: Rock and stone no longer bothered his feet
quiz.explanation: He walked barefoot so often that his feet became hardened to rock and stone.

cards.title: Babur carved a reminder of death on a rock beside a spring
cards.body:
In summer 1502, retreating before Shaibani Khan into the Macha hills, Babur came to a spring with a tomb beside it. Following a local custom of cutting verses into rocks, he had a stone shaped and carved with lines about the legendary Persian king Jamshid: many men like us have rested at this spring and passed away in the blink of an eye; we took the world by courage and might, but did not take it with us to the tomb.

He was nineteen, homeless and still hungry for a throne, yet he chose these words. Ambition and humility can live together, and remembering that nothing goes with us to the grave helps us hold success and failure more lightly.
cards.quote: We took the world by courage and might, But we took it not with us to the tomb.
cards.apply_it: Write down one thing you are striving for. Then add one line on what will matter about it when you are gone.

quiz.question: What did Babur have carved on a rock at a mountain spring?
options: Verses saying the world cannot be taken to the tomb
quiz.explanation: The lines about Jamshid say that those who conquered the world did not take it with them to the grave.

cards.title: At his lowest, Babur planned to run away to China
cards.body:
In 1502 Babur lived in Tashkent at the court of his uncle, the Mongol Khan. Most of his men had scattered, and those who stayed were too poor to ride with him, so he sometimes went to the Khan's court with only one or two attendants. Feeling the poverty and humiliation sharply, he resolved to slip away eastward, as far as China, which he had always wanted to see. He told no one, partly because his companions had chosen exile for his sake and he could not bear to tell them.

Many people who later achieve much pass through a season like this. Wanting to run is not failure. The plan never happened, and within two years Babur ruled Kabul.
cards.quote: better to go as far as my feet can carry me than be seen of men in such poverty and humiliation.
cards.apply_it: If you are in a low season, write down one thing you still have, one person who has stayed with you, and one small step you can take.

quiz.question: Where did Babur plan to escape to during his poverty in Tashkent?
quiz.explanation: He had long wanted to visit China and resolved to go there, though the plan was overtaken by events.

cards.title: Hunted and alone, Babur wrote that nothing is worse than fear for your life
cards.body:
In 1503, after his uncles' campaign in Ferghana collapsed, Babur was driven out of Akhsi by his rival Tambal's men. With his horse worn out, he fled into the hills with two pursuers who swore on the Quran to serve him, then seemed to lead him astray. Hiding in an orchard near Karnan in a borrowed sheepskin coat, he learned that riders had been sent to seize him. He walked to a corner of the garden to prepare for death, and there his narrative breaks off mid-sentence. Somehow he survived.

His honesty about terror is striking for a warrior-king. Fear is not shameful. Even the bravest feel it, and naming it is the start of facing it.
cards.quote: nothing in the world is worse than fear for one's life
cards.apply_it: Write down a fear you have been avoiding naming. Seeing it in words often makes it easier to face.

quiz.question: What is unusual about Babur's account of his flight from Akhsi in 1503?
options: He claims he was never afraid
He admits his terror, and the text breaks off as he prepares for death
He says he defeated Tambal alone
quiz.explanation: He wrote openly about fear for his life; the surviving text stops mid-sentence at that moment.

cards.title: From two tents to a kingdom: Babur's fresh start in Kabul
cards.body:
In June 1504, aged twenty-one, Babur left the Ferghana Valley for good with two or three hundred followers, most on foot with walking sticks, and so few tents that his own went to his mother. Heading south, his band swelled as soldiers deserted the local strongman Khusrau Shah. In October 1504 the ruler of Kabul surrendered the city without a fight. When a mob threatened the departing ruler's family, Babur rode out, had several rioters shot or cut down, and saw them leave safely.

Kabul, in today's Afghanistan, became his base for twenty years and the place he loved most. Losing the home you planned on can open the way to the life you actually build.
cards.quote: without a fight, without an effort, by Almighty God's bounty and mercy, I obtained and made subject to me Kābul and Ghaznī and their dependent districts.
cards.locator: Section II. Kābul[666]. 910 Ah.-june 14Th 1504 to June 4Th 1505 Ad.[667] ¶46
cards.apply_it: Think of a door that closed on you. List one thing that became possible only because it closed.

quiz.question: How did Babur gain Kabul in October 1504?
options: He inherited it from his father
Its ruler surrendered without a fight
He bought it from the Persians
quiz.explanation: He writes that he obtained Kabul and Ghazni without a fight or an effort.

cards.title: Babur admitted his first tax in Kabul hurt the country
cards.body:
Kabul was a small, poor country, and in 1504 it was suddenly crowded with clans who had followed Babur from Samarkand, Hisar and Kunduz. To feed their families, he levied 30,000 donkey-loads of grain on Kabul, Ghazni and their districts. He later wrote that he knew nothing about the harvests at the time, that the demand was excessive, and that the country suffered very badly under it.

Rulers rarely record that their own policy hurt people. Babur did. When you make a decision without good information, say so afterwards, find out the real numbers, and let the lesson shape the next decision.
cards.quote: we knew nothing at that time about the harvests and incomings; the impost was excessive, and under it the country suffered very grievously.
cards.apply_it: Recall a decision you made on too little information. Write down what you know now that you didn't then.

quiz.question: What did Babur say was wrong with his grain levy on Kabul?
options: It was excessive, made without knowing the harvests, and caused great suffering
It was too small to help
It was paid only by merchants
quiz.explanation: He admitted he did not know the harvests and that the impost made the country suffer grievously.

cards.title: After losing his mother, Babur mourned with others before taking heart
cards.body:
In June 1505, a few months after he took Kabul, Babur's mother Qutluq-nigar Khanim fell ill with fever and died within six days. She had shared most of his years of wandering. He and a friend carried her to a garden on the mountainside and buried her there. While they were still mourning, news came of the deaths of his grandmother and an uncle, and when more relatives arrived from Khurasan the grief broke out afresh.

Babur describes what helped: the customary rites, food given to the poor, prayers, and family gathered together. Grief does not need to be rushed. Shared rituals and company can help us, slowly, take heart again.
cards.quote: When the mourning-rites had been observed, food and victuals set out for the poor and destitute, the Qorān recited, and prayers offered for the departed souls, we steadied ourselves and all took heart again.
cards.apply_it: If you are grieving, consider one small shared ritual, like a meal, a walk or lighting a candle, with someone who also misses them.

quiz.question: What helped Babur and his family steady themselves after his mother's death?
options: Forbidding anyone to speak of her
Mourning rites, feeding the poor, prayers and being together
quiz.explanation: He lists the rites, food for the poor and prayers, after which they took heart again.

cards.title: Herat's charming princes were strangers to war, and lost everything
cards.body:
In 1506 Babur travelled to Herat, in today's western Afghanistan, to join the sons of the late Timurid ruler Sultan Husain Mirza against Shaibani Khan. Herat was a dazzling centre of poetry, music and painting, and the princes gave elegant parties. Babur enjoyed their company but judged them sharply: it took them three months just to leave the city, agree among themselves and gather troops. In 1507 Shaibani Khan marched in, and the city's notables went out to hand him the keys.

Charm and good company are real gifts, but they cannot replace preparation. Whatever you are responsible for, make sure it can survive a real test, not only make a good impression.
cards.quote: The Mīrzās were good enough as company and in social matters, in conversation and parties, but they were strangers to war, strategy, equipment, bold fight and encounter.
cards.apply_it: Pick one thing you are responsible for. Ask: if it were tested tomorrow, what is the weakest part? Spend 20 minutes on that.

quiz.question: What was Babur's verdict on the princes of Herat?
options: Good company, but strangers to war and strategy
Too poor to raise an army
quiz.explanation: He found them fine in conversation and at parties but unready for war, and Herat soon fell to the Uzbeks.

cards.title: Notice the moment you start talking yourself into something
cards.body:
Until his twenties Babur did not drink. As a boy he refused wine even when his father pressed it on him, and his religious teacher kept him from it. At Herat in 1506, surrounded by refined parties and pressed by his hosts, he felt the pull and caught himself reasoning: where should I drink, if not here? That time he found a polite excuse and held back, though in later years he did take up wine.

Temptation usually arrives with a convincing argument attached. Learning to recognise your own favourite justifications, like 'just this once' or 'where better than here?', gives you a moment to choose.
cards.quote: Where should I drink if not here? here where all the chattels and utensils of luxury and comfort are gathered and in use.
cards.apply_it: Write down the phrase you most often use to talk yourself into a habit you want to avoid. Next time you hear it in your head, pause.

quiz.question: What argument did Babur catch himself using at Herat?
options: My father would want me to
Where should I drink if not here, amid all this luxury?
quiz.explanation: The refinement of Herat made drinking feel justified; he noticed the reasoning and, that time, held back.

cards.title: In a blizzard, Babur refused a warm cave while his men froze
cards.body:
Crossing the mountains from Herat to Kabul in the winter of 1506 to 1507, Babur's army was trapped in deep snow. For a week he took turns with ten or fifteen others stamping down a path, sinking to waist or chest. At a cave, in a violent blizzard, his companions urged him inside. He dug a hole in the snow at the entrance instead, unwilling to sleep warm while his men suffered outside, and sat there until snow lay thick on his head and back. Only when someone found the cave had room for everyone did he go in.

People follow those who share their conditions. Small acts of solidarity carry more weight than speeches.
cards.quote: Whatever hardship and wretchedness there is, I will face; what strong men stand, I will stand
cards.apply_it: Find one unglamorous task your team is stuck with this week and do a share of it yourself.

quiz.question: Why did Babur stay outside the cave in the blizzard?
options: He would not shelter in comfort while his men suffered in the snow
He was keeping watch for enemies
The cave was full of animals
quiz.explanation: He felt it would be no act of comradeship to sleep warm while his men were out in the storm.

cards.title: The deep snow that nearly killed them also carried them through
cards.body:
After the night in the cave, Babur's men took a route straight down an unknown valley instead of the usual road over the pass. That night many lost hands or feet to frostbite. Yet when they came out, no one in the region could remember anyone crossing in such snow. Babur saw the irony: the very depth of the snow had made those pathless slopes and sudden drops passable.

He summed it up in a line: everything, good and bad, is gain if looked at rightly. That does not deny real suffering. It invites us to look for what a hard thing also made possible.
cards.quote: All ill, all good in the count, is gain if looked at aright!
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent difficulty. Write one thing it made possible that would not have happened otherwise.

quiz.question: How did the deep snow help Babur's army in the end?
options: It hid them from the enemy
It stopped the Uzbeks from following
It made steep, pathless slopes passable
quiz.explanation: Babur reasoned that without the deep snow they could not have crossed those pathless slopes and drops.

cards.title: At Qandahar, Babur won by organising his men in tens and fifties
cards.body:
In 1507 Babur fought the Arghun brothers who held Qandahar, in southern Afghanistan. His army was smaller, and many soldiers had scattered in search of food and water. But he had organised his own guard better than ever before: men listed in tens and fifties, each group under a leader who knew its post and its job, so they could charge without anyone needing to marshal them. At one point only eleven men remained beside him, yet he advanced and the enemy fled. That same year he began styling himself Padshah, emperor, instead of Mirza.

Small units with clear roles let a team act fast under pressure. Structure is what makes courage usable.
cards.quote: Though our men were few I had them organized and posted on a first-rate plan and method; I had never arrayed them before by such a good one.
cards.apply_it: For your next group project, give each person or small group one clearly named role before work begins.

quiz.question: What gave Babur's small force its edge at Qandahar in 1507?
options: Organisation into tens and fifties, each with a leader who knew its job
quiz.explanation: Clear small units with known posts let his men act without being marshalled in the heat of battle.

cards.title: Before thirty, Babur had won and lost Samarkand three times
cards.body:
In 1510 Shah Ismail of Persia defeated and killed Shaibani Khan, and Babur saw his chance. With Persian help he marched north and, in October 1511, re-entered Samarkand to cheering crowds. But his alliance with the Shia Shah made him distrusted by the Sunni Uzbeks and many townspeople. In spring 1512, against cautious advice, he attacked the Uzbek leader Ubaid Khan with a small force at Kul-i-malik, was defeated, and left Samarkand for good. His translator, Annette Beveridge, notes that after all these gains and losses he was still under thirty.

It is easy to feel that one setback defines a life. Babur's greatest achievement still lay ahead.
cards.quote: After experiencing such gains and such losses, Bābur was still under 30 years of age.
cards.apply_it: Write down your age and the biggest setback you have had. Then write one thing you still hope to do. There is time.

quiz.question: How many times had Babur taken Samarkand by 1511?
quiz.explanation: He took it in 1497, 1500 and 1511, and lost it each time.

cards.title: In his Garden of Fidelity, Babur stopped to savour one autumn
cards.body:
In 1508 to 1509 Babur laid out a four-part garden near Adinapur, close to today's Jalalabad in eastern Afghanistan, and named it the Bagh-i-Wafa, the Garden of Fidelity. He planted oranges and pomegranates around a pool ringed with clover, and later sugar-cane and bananas brought from India. In October 1519 he stayed there for a few days at its peak and wrote down exactly what he saw: lawns of clover, pomegranates turning gold, oranges still green.

A king who spent most of his life on campaign made time to notice one perfect season. Savouring means slowing down long enough to see the details while they last.
cards.quote: Those were the days of the garden's beauty; its lawns were one sheet of trefoil; its pomegranate-trees yellowed to autumn splendour
cards.apply_it: Visit a park or garden this week and describe three specific details in writing, as Babur did.

quiz.question: What did Babur call the garden he made near Adinapur?
quiz.explanation: The Bagh-i-Wafa, or Garden of Fidelity, was laid out in 1508 to 1509.

cards.title: Babur once counted 32 kinds of tulips on the hills near Kabul
cards.body:
Describing the country around Kabul, Babur stops to talk about wildflowers. Tulips of many colours covered the foothills, and he once counted 32 or 33 different sorts. He and his companions named one the Rose-scented, because its perfume was a little like a red rose's, and he noted that another, the Hundred-leaved tulip, grew in just one spot, below Parwan at the mouth of the Ghurband narrows.

This is a warrior-king paying the kind of close attention we usually give to screens. Naming and counting what grows around you is a simple way to be present, and it turns an ordinary walk into a discovery.
cards.quote: Tulips of many colours cover these foot-hills; I once counted them up; it came out at 32 or 33 different sorts.
cards.apply_it: On your next walk, count how many different kinds of one thing you see, whether flowers, trees or birds.

quiz.question: How many kinds of tulip did Babur count in the foothills near Kabul?
quiz.explanation: He once counted 32 or 33 different sorts and even named one the Rose-scented.

cards.title: Babur's wife asked to raise his next child as her own, boy or girl
cards.body:
Babur's wife Maham was the mother of his heir Humayun, born in Kabul in March 1508, but several of her later children had died. In January 1519, while Babur was campaigning, she wrote asking that the next child born to another of his wives be given to her to bring up, whether a boy or a girl. Babur agreed in writing before the baby was born. When news of a son's birth arrived during his march into India, he named him Hindal.

Families in many times and places have made room for children through adoption and shared care. What makes a parent is the choice to take a child into your heart and keeping.
cards.quote: Whether it be a boy, whether it be a girl, is my luck and chance; give it to me; I will declare it my child and will take charge of it.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who cared for you though they didn't have to, like a step-parent, aunt or mentor. Tell them what it meant.

quiz.question: What did Maham ask Babur for in 1519?
options: To raise the next child born to another wife as her own
quiz.explanation: She asked to adopt the unborn child, boy or girl; Babur agreed, and the boy was named Hindal.

cards.title: In 1519 Babur stormed Bajaur, then ordered his army to harm no one at Bhira
cards.body:
Babur's first serious move toward India in 1519 shows two faces of conquest. In January his army stormed the fort of Bajaur, in today's northwest Pakistan, using matchlock guns its defenders had never seen. By his own account more than 3,000 men were killed and their wives and children taken captive. Weeks later, near Bhira on the Jhelum river, land once ruled by Timur's descendants, he ordered that the local people and their flocks be left completely unharmed, because he hoped to rule them.

The contrast is uncomfortable, and worth facing. How the powerful treat people often depends on whether they see them as 'theirs'. A fair test of character is how we treat those we don't need.
cards.quote: Do no hurt or harm to the flocks and herds of these people, nor even to their cotton-ends and broken needles!
cards.apply_it: Notice how you treat someone this week who can do nothing for you, such as a stranger, a cold caller or a new colleague.

quiz.question: Why did Babur order his army not to harm the people around Bhira?
options: They had paid him a large ransom in advance
He saw the land as rightfully his and hoped to rule it
A treaty with Persia forbade it
quiz.explanation: He pictured these lands, once held by Timur's line, as his own, so it was imperative to treat the people well.

cards.title: Babur gave up mocking verses after feeling they cheapened him
cards.body:
Babur was a gifted poet who loved quick, joking verse. While writing the Mubin, a long serious poem on religious duty, he was struck by a thought: what a pity if a tongue that had expressed such lofty things went back to wasting itself on low words. He resolved to give up satire and coarse jokes. Then, in December 1525, on a raft heading toward India, he dashed off a teasing couplet about a companion. Days later he fell ill and coughed blood, and he took it as a rebuke.

Whatever we make of the illness, his point stands: the words we use for cheap laughs shape who we become.
cards.quote: A pity it ... will be if the tongue which has treasure of utterances so lofty as these are, waste itself again on low words
cards.locator: Section III. Hindūstān. 932 Ah.-oct. 18Th 1525 to Oct. 8Th 1526 Ad.[1565] ¶17
cards.apply_it: For one day, notice any joke you make at someone else's expense. Replace one of them with a genuine compliment.

quiz.question: Why did Babur decide to give up satirical and jesting verse?
options: He felt a tongue that had written lofty things should not waste itself on low words
quiz.explanation: Writing the Mubin made him feel that cheap, mocking verse was beneath what his words could do.

cards.title: Babur held his grown son to account, firmly and in writing
cards.body:
In late 1525, as Babur gathered his army at the Garden of Fidelity for his fifth expedition into India, his eldest son Humayun, then seventeen and governor of Badakhshan, arrived long after the agreed date. Babur wrote him harsh letters and, when he finally came, spoke to him very severely. In 1527, when Humayun opened treasure-houses in Delhi without permission, Babur again sent stern reproaches, writing that he had never expected such a thing from him and that it grieved him very much.

Love does not mean letting things slide. Clear expectations, named honestly when they are broken, help young adults learn that their actions matter.
cards.quote: I wrote harsh letters to Humāyūn, lecturing him severely because of his long delay beyond the time fixed for him to join me.
cards.locator: Section III. Hindūstān. 932 Ah.-oct. 18Th 1525 to Oct. 8Th 1526 Ad.[1565] ¶7
cards.apply_it: If someone you guide has broken an agreement, tell them plainly and kindly what you expected, what happened, and what you need next time.

quiz.question: Why did Babur write harsh letters to Humayun in 1525?
options: Humayun was long overdue to join the army
quiz.explanation: Humayun's long delay past the agreed time drew a severe rebuke from his father.

cards.title: Babur said it was no shame for his soldiers to be afraid
cards.body:
Camped at Panipat, north of Delhi, in April 1526, many of Babur's men were frightened. Babur believed worry could not change what God had already decided, yet he refused to blame them. They were two or three months' march from home, facing a vast army of people whose language none of them spoke. In those conditions, he wrote, fear was no disgrace.

Good leaders don't shame people for natural feelings. They name the real reasons for fear, show they understand, and then give people something solid to stand on: in Babur's case, a carefully fortified position and a clear plan. Acknowledging fear often steadies people more than denying it.
cards.quote: But though this is so, it was no reproach to be afraid and anxious.
cards.locator: Section III. Hindūstān. 932 Ah.-oct. 18Th 1525 to Oct. 8Th 1526 Ad.[1565] ¶108
cards.apply_it: When someone on your team is anxious, first name the real reason their worry makes sense, then share the plan.

quiz.question: How did Babur view his soldiers' fear before Panipat?
options: As understandable, given how far they were from home among strangers
As a sign the battle was lost
quiz.explanation: He wrote that it was no reproach to be afraid, given the distance from home and an unfamiliar people.

cards.title: At Panipat in 1526, preparation beat numbers and began an empire
cards.body:
In April 1526, at Panipat, north of Delhi, Babur faced Sultan Ibrahim Lodi, whose army was put at 100,000 men and about 1,000 elephants. Babur's force, counting servants, was around 12,000. He anchored one flank on the town, had 700 carts lashed together with rawhide ropes in the Ottoman style, placed matchlock men and cannon behind them, and sent horsemen to wheel round the enemy's flanks. By noon Ibrahim's army was crushed and Ibrahim lay dead. Babur estimated 15,000 or more killed, and later heard it may have been 40,000 or 50,000.

The battle began the Mughal Empire. Careful preparation and new tools can outweigh sheer size, but victory still carries a terrible human cost.
cards.quote: In one half-day, that armed mass was laid upon the earth.
cards.locator: Section III. Hindūstān. 932 Ah.-oct. 18Th 1525 to Oct. 8Th 1526 Ad.[1565] ¶121
cards.apply_it: Facing a challenge bigger than you? List three ways to prepare the ground in your favour before the decisive moment.

quiz.question: What did Babur use to fortify his front line at Panipat?
options: About 700 carts tied together, with matchlock men and cannon behind them
quiz.explanation: Carts joined in the Ottoman fashion sheltered his gunners, while flanking parties encircled the enemy.

cards.title: Humayun offered his father a famous diamond, and Babur gave it back
cards.body:
After Panipat, Humayun rode ahead to Agra. The family of the Raja of Gwalior, who had died fighting for Ibrahim, gave him a hoard of jewels. Among them was a famous diamond, said by appraisers to be worth two and a half days' food for the whole world, which many historians identify with the Koh-i-Noor. When Babur reached Agra, Humayun dutifully offered it to him. Babur simply gave it back.

One line in the memoir holds a whole relationship. Letting a child keep the credit and reward for what they achieved tells them you trust them and are proud of them, without a speech.
cards.quote: Humāyūn offered it to me when I arrived at Āgra; I just gave it him back.
cards.locator: Section III. Hindūstān. 932 Ah.-oct. 18Th 1525 to Oct. 8Th 1526 Ad.[1565] ¶140
cards.apply_it: When someone you care for shares a success, let them keep the credit fully. Resist adding advice or comparisons.

quiz.question: What did Babur do with the great diamond Humayun offered him?
options: Sold it to pay the army
quiz.explanation: Babur records simply that he gave it back to his son.

cards.title: When his officers wanted to go home, Babur let the unwilling leave
cards.body:
Agra in the hot season of 1526 was miserable for Babur's army. The townspeople had fled, food was scarce, the roads were unsafe, and a deadly heat struck men down in heaps. Many officers, even his old friend Khwaja Kalan, wanted to return to Kabul. Babur called a council. He reminded them how much hardship had gone into winning these lands and asked why they should give them up to go back to poverty in Kabul. Then he gave a clear choice: no more talk of leaving, but anyone without the will to stay was free to go. Khwaja Kalan went; most stayed.

A firm decision paired with an honest exit is better than a half-committed team.
cards.quote: Henceforth, let no well-wisher of mine speak of such things! But let not those turn back from going who, weak in strong persistence, have set their faces to depart!
cards.apply_it: If your team keeps reopening a settled decision, restate it clearly, and offer a respectful way out for anyone who can't commit.

quiz.question: How did Babur handle officers who wanted to leave India in 1526?
options: He agreed to return to Kabul
He bribed them all to stay
He forbade talk of leaving but let the unwilling go
quiz.explanation: He ended the debate but allowed those who lacked the will to stay, like Khwaja Kalan, to depart.

cards.title: Babur found India 'a different world' and set out to describe it
cards.body:
Crossing the Indus, Babur felt he had entered another world: different mountains, rivers, plants, animals, seasons, peoples and languages. He filled long pages with careful notes on rhinoceroses and elephants, mangoes and flowers, the seasons of heat, rain and cold, and Indian ways of measuring weight and time. He loved the rains and admired the country's countless skilled craftsmen.

He also wrote harsh, sweeping complaints about India, shaped by homesickness and a conqueror's outlook; they say more about him than about India. The better part of his response is the curiosity. When a place feels foreign, studying it closely is the first step toward understanding it.
cards.quote: Compared with our countries it is a different world; its mountains, rivers, jungles and deserts, its towns, its cultivated lands, its animals and plants, its peoples and their tongues, its rains, and its winds, are all different.
cards.apply_it: Next time you are somewhere unfamiliar, write down five things that are different from home before judging any of them.

quiz.question: Which of these did Babur praise in India?
options: Its rains and its countless skilled workmen
quiz.explanation: He found the air in the rains remarkably fine and admired India's endless artisans.

cards.title: Homesick in Agra, Babur built gardens with running water
cards.body:
What Babur missed most in India was running water and orderly gardens. Soon after reaching Agra in 1526 he crossed the Yamuna river to look for land, and found ground so ugly that he nearly gave up the idea. He built anyway: a great well, tanks, a bath-house of red stone as a refuge from heat, wind and dust, and garden plots laid out symmetrically with roses and narcissus. His officers soon began laying out gardens of their own along the river.

When you can't go home, you can bring some of home to where you are. Shaping your surroundings, even a balcony or a corner, is a practical way to settle into a new place.
cards.quote: it kept coming to my mind that waters should be made to flow by means of wheels erected wherever I might settle down, also that grounds should be laid out in an orderly and symmetrical way.
cards.apply_it: Add one thing from 'home', a plant, a photo or a familiar smell, to the space where you spend most of your day.

quiz.question: What did Babur do about the lack of running water he disliked in India?
options: He built wells, water-wheels, tanks and symmetrical gardens
He ordered rivers diverted through Delhi
quiz.explanation: He laid out gardens with flowing water at Agra, and his officers followed his example.

cards.title: Surviving poison taught Babur how sweet life can be
cards.body:
In December 1526 Babur ate a dish of hare and fell sick. Investigation showed that the mother of the defeated Sultan Ibrahim had bribed a taster and the kitchen cooks to poison his food. By luck, only part of the poison was sprinkled on one dish and most was thrown into the fire. Babur recovered over several days on milk and remedies. Writing to Kabul, he said he had never known so well how sweet life could seem.

A brush with death often clears away what doesn't matter. We don't need a crisis to learn that lesson; a few quiet moments of gratitude for simply being alive can do some of the same work.
cards.quote: Till now I had not known so well how sweet a thing life can seem!
cards.apply_it: Tonight, before sleep, spend one minute simply noticing that you are alive and breathing, and name one thing you are glad of.

quiz.question: What did Babur write after surviving the poisoning attempt in 1526?
options: That he had never known so well how sweet life can seem
That he would execute all his cooks
That he would never eat again
quiz.explanation: The near-death experience made him feel the worth of life more keenly than ever.

cards.title: Babur quit drinking by breaking every cup and telling everyone
cards.body:
In the years after Herat, Babur had become a regular drinker; his diaries are full of wine parties. On 25 February 1527, riding out as the army prepared to face Rana Sanga, he reflected that he had always wished to stop and that the habit had left a lasting stain on his heart. He vowed to give up wine. He had his gold and silver cups and flagons broken up and the pieces given to the poor, had the wine poured out, and ordered a well and an almshouse built on the spot. About 300 officers and men joined his vow.

Big changes stick better when you remove temptation, make the decision public and give it a good purpose. Babur did all three in one day.
cards.quote: Thus eased I my heart by renouncement of wine.
cards.apply_it: Pick one habit you want to drop. Remove one source of temptation from your home today and tell one person about your decision.

quiz.question: What did Babur do with his gold and silver drinking vessels when he gave up wine?
options: Had them broken up and the pieces given to the poor
quiz.explanation: The fragments went to deserving people and dervishes, and a well with an almshouse marked the spot.

cards.title: Before Khanwa, Babur steadied a frightened army with a call to honour
cards.body:
In early 1527 Rana Sanga of Chittor, a Rajput ruler who, Babur admits, had grown great by his own courage, advanced with a large army. Babur's advance troops were beaten, an astrologer was predicting defeat, and his men were losing heart. Babur gathered his officers and spoke of death and reputation: everyone dies, so a good name matters more than a long life. They swore on the Quran not to turn back. On 17 March 1527, at Khanwa, west of Agra, his carts and guns held and the Rajput army was broken. Afterwards Babur had a tower of the slain men's heads raised on a hill.

Shared purpose can steady people in fear, though the same fervour can also excuse cruelty.
cards.quote: Better than life with a bad name, is death with a good one.
cards.locator: Farmān Announcing Bābur's Renunciation of Wine.[2022] ¶13
cards.apply_it: When your group is losing heart, remind them of the 'why' behind the work before you talk about the 'how'.

quiz.question: How did Babur restore his army's morale before Khanwa?
options: He spoke of dying with a good name, and they swore an oath not to retreat
He promised to return to Kabul
quiz.explanation: His speech on honour and the oath on the Quran stiffened the army's resolve.

cards.title: Babur told his son to write plainly, to spare the reader trouble
cards.body:
In November 1528 Babur wrote a long letter to Humayun, then governing Badakhshan. He opened with joy at the birth of Humayun's son. Then, amid news and advice, he gave very direct feedback on Humayun's own letters: they were so ornate they read like riddles, the spelling had slips, and if Humayun had read them over he would surely have changed them. His advice was to drop the elaboration and use plain, clear words, which would save trouble for writer and reader alike.

It is still the best writing advice there is. It also shows a parent giving specific, practical feedback rather than vague praise or blame.
cards.quote: In future write without elaboration; use plain, clear words. So will thy trouble and thy reader's be less.
cards.locator: Copy of a Letter to Humāyūn.[2350] ¶16
cards.apply_it: Reread the next important message you write before sending it, and cut every word that makes it harder to understand.

quiz.question: What writing advice did Babur give Humayun?
options: Drop the elaboration and use plain, clear words
quiz.explanation: He said plain words would make things easier for both the writer and the reader.

cards.title: Babur urged his son not to retreat into solitude
cards.body:
Humayun's letters kept talking about 'retirement', wanting to withdraw from the business of rule. Babur answered firmly that retirement does not go with ruling; no bondage equals that of sovereignty. He told his son to stop sitting alone and avoiding company, to call his younger brother and his officers to him twice a day, and to settle every decision in counsel with experienced advisers.

Withdrawing can be a sign of being overwhelmed rather than lazy. Babur's remedy was structure and connection: regular meetings and trusted people close by. For anyone carrying responsibility, isolation makes things harder, not easier.
cards.quote: If thou seek to pleasure me, give up sitting alone and avoiding society.
cards.locator: Copy of a Letter to Humāyūn.[2350] ¶17
cards.apply_it: If you've been pulling away from people, schedule one short, regular check-in with someone you trust this week.

quiz.question: What did Babur advise Humayun to do instead of withdrawing?
options: Meet his brother and officers twice daily and decide matters in counsel
quiz.explanation: Babur prescribed regular company and shared decision-making as the cure for withdrawal.

cards.title: Two years after quitting wine, the craving still brought Babur near tears
cards.body:
Babur did not pretend that giving up wine was easy. In February 1529, two years after his vow, he wrote to his old friend Khwaja Kalan that his longing for a wine party had been endless, so strong at times that it brought him close to tears. This year, he said, it had finally eased, perhaps helped by a demanding poetry project: putting a religious treatise into verse. He even urged his friend to give up wine too.

Cravings after quitting a habit are normal and can last a long time. Honesty about them, and a demanding project to pour energy into, can help them fade. If a habit is hard to shift, support from others makes a real difference.
cards.quote: the longing and craving for a wine-party has been infinite and endless for two years past, so much so that sometimes the craving for wine brought me to the verge of tears.
cards.locator: Copy of a Letter to Humāyūn.[2350] ¶104
cards.apply_it: If you're breaking a habit, choose one absorbing project to turn to when the urge comes, and tell one person how it's really going.

quiz.question: According to Babur, what may have helped his craving for wine finally ease?
quiz.explanation: He credited, in part, the blessing of turning a religious tract into verse.

cards.title: The emperor of Hindustan wept over a melon from home
cards.body:
By 1529 Babur ruled from the Indus to Bihar, yet his heart kept turning back to Kabul. In the same letter to Khwaja Kalan he wrote that his desire to return was boundless. When a melon from those northern lands was brought to him, cutting and eating it moved him so strangely that he was all tears. Later that year, when a melon-grower from Balkh raised good melons in Agra and grapes ripened on vines in his garden, he said it filled his measure of content.

Success does not cancel longing. Admitting that you miss a place or a person is not weakness; even the most successful people carry somewhere they call home.
cards.quote: a melon was brought to me; to cut and eat it affected me strangely; I was all tears!
cards.locator: Copy of a Letter to Humāyūn.[2350] ¶99
cards.apply_it: Cook or eat something that tastes of a place you miss, and share the story behind it with someone.

quiz.question: What brought Babur to tears in India in 1529?
options: Eating a melon from his homeland
quiz.explanation: A melon from the northern lands stirred such longing for home that he wept.

cards.title: Babur's last counsel: never act against your brothers
cards.body:
In 1530 Humayun fell dangerously ill with fever. According to Babur's daughter Gulbadan and later chroniclers, when the doctors could do nothing, Babur walked three times around his son's bed, praying to give his own life in exchange. Humayun recovered; Babur fell ill and died in Agra on 26 December 1530, aged forty-seven. Before he died he named Humayun his successor and, as the historian Abu'l-Fazl reports, urged him to be generous and just, to forgive, and above all to do nothing against his brothers, even if they deserved it.

Whether or not the vow worked, the story shows how his family remembered his love. His final counsel was about holding the family together.
cards.quote: the cream of my testamentary dispositions is this, 'Do naught against your brothers, even though they may deserve it.'
cards.locator: Translator's Note on 936 to 937 Ah.-1529 to 1530 Ad ¶54
cards.apply_it: Is there a family rift you could soften? Take one small step, a message or a kind word, even if you feel you are in the right.

quiz.question: According to Abu'l-Fazl, what was the heart of Babur's dying advice to Humayun?
options: Do nothing against your brothers, even if they deserve it
quiz.explanation: He called it the cream of his last wishes: do naught against your brothers.
